         B.       ISO-NE’s TCS Process

                 1.       Order No. 2023 and the Shift from Individual to Cluster Study

        ISO-NE historically studied each Interconnection Customer’s interconnection request

individually, in serial queue order (“Serial Study”). In Order No. 2023, the Commission directed

ISO-NE to transition from this “first-come, first-served” Serial Study approach to a “first-ready,

first-served” cluster study model (“Cluster Study”).12 Order No. 2023 also required ISO-NE to

conduct a TCS before beginning Cluster Studies. The TCS process is similar in many ways to the

Cluster Study. Notably, the Cluster Study nominally uses the same study methodology as the

TCS. However, the TCS has some key differences. First, TCS Interconnection Customers must

make a $5,000,000 deposit prior to entering the TCS.13 Second, after issuance of the TCS Final

Report, Interconnection Customers must execute an LGIA and provide a 20% deposit for the

identified Upgrades or will be deemed withdrawn.14 Third, a TCS Interconnection Customer may

incur a Transitional Withdrawal Penalty “equal to nine (9) times Interconnection Customer’s

total study cost incurred since entering the System Operator’s interconnection queue” if it

withdraws its Interconnection Request or “otherwise does not reach Commercial Operation.”15

                 2.       Description of TCS

Capability Interconnection Standard (“CCIS”)16 and ISO-NE Planning Procedure 5-6 (“PP5-

Rather, the Complaint targets a broad problem with how ISO-NE implemented its Transitional

I.   Introduction, Qualifications, Assignment, and Summary of Opinions

     A.     Witness Qualifications

1.   My name is Danielle S. Powers. I am a mechanical engineer and Chief Executive Officer
     of Concentric Energy Advisors, Inc. (“Concentric”). My business address is 293 Boston
     Post Road West, Suite 500, Marlborough, MA 01752.

2.   I have over thirty-five years of direct experience in the public utility industry. I have
     worked for an investor-owned utility, an independent system operator, and most recently
     as a consultant. I have managed and/or participated in a wide variety of consulting
     engagements as an expert in wholesale market design, power system operations, as well
     as resource planning. I have provided expert testimony or reports before the Indiana
     Utility Regulatory Commission, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Illinois
     Commerce Commission, the Connecticut Siting Council, the Massachusetts District
     Court, the Regulatory Commission of Alaska, the New York Public Service Commission,
     the United States Bankruptcy Court, the Missouri House Utilities Committee, and the
     Indiana Senate Utilities Committee. My previous testimony has typically addressed
     issues related to wholesale energy market design, transmission policy, and resource
     planning.

3.   My name is Mark G. Karl. I am an aero-mechanical engineer currently working as an
     Executive Advisor at Concentric. My business address is 293 Boston Post Road West,
     Suite 500, Marlborough, MA 01752.

4.   I have over four decades of energy industry experience, with a tenured history of
     operations in the wholesale electric market from design to implementation, including
     resource adequacy. Before joining Concentric, I spent over 23 years at ISO New England
     Inc. (“ISO-NE”), where I most recently served as the Vice President of Market
     Development and Settlements. In that role I held executive-level responsibility for the
     design, development, and implementation of all changes to the wholesale electricity
     markets operated by ISO-NE, overseeing the entire process from inception to
     implementation, including stakeholder and regulatory processes as well as operations and
     settlements. I previously held leadership positions in Resource Adequacy, Market
     Development and Integration, and Market Design. Prior to my tenure at ISO-NE, I spent
     nearly 20 years at an investor-owned utility with positions in generation engineering and
     operations, system planning, project development, regulatory and economic analysis and
     finance.

     B.     Assignment

5.   Concentric was asked to evaluate ISO-NE’s methodology and analytical framework for
     conducting the Transitional Cluster Study (“TCS”), including the manner in which ISO-
     NE applied its Network Capability Interconnection Standard (“NCIS”) and Capacity
     Capability Interconnection Standard (“CCIS”) analyses in the transition from a serial
                                     PUBLIC VERSION
                                                                                Attachment B
                                                               Moraga Storage, et al. v. ISO-NE
                                                                          Concentric Affidavit
                                                                                   Page 3 of 53

     interconnection process to a cluster study process. Our review included whether the TCS
     methodology appropriately identifies the transmission facilities incrementally required to
     provide the interconnection service requested by TCS participants and distinguishes those
     requirements from pre-existing system conditions, transmission limitations, and other
     transmission needs.

6.   We were also asked to evaluate the resulting assignment of Network Upgrade costs to
     TCS participants, the transparency and reproducibility of the study results, the
     implications of the TCS process for participating projects, and potential methodological
     and transitional remedies that would preserve reliability and existing transmission and
     capacity rights while ensuring that TCS participants are assigned only those transmission
     upgrades and costs properly attributable to their requested interconnection service.

     C.     Summary of Opinions

7.   The TCS does not utilize incremental cost causation. A sound interconnection analysis
     should answer three related questions in sequence: (i) whether a transmission limitation
     or need exists under the conditions being studied; (ii) whether, and to what extent, that
     need is incrementally caused by the interconnection requests under study; and (iii) only
     after the incremental need has been identified, how the cost of the required upgrade
     should be allocated among the projects that cause or contribute to it. The principal
     concerns with the TCS arise at the first two steps. ISO-NE’s methodology identifies
     whether TCS projects contribute to loading on a constrained facility, but ISO-NE’s
     provided data does not reliably establish that the full scope of every resulting capacity-
     related upgrade is incrementally required “but for” those projects.

8.   A new resource seeking Capacity Network Resource Interconnection Service (“CNRIS”)
     should not obtain capacity deliverability by assuming that an existing resource will
     surrender transmission capability already associated with its capacity rights. Stressed
     system conditions are therefore an appropriate part of a CCIS analysis. The issue is
     whether the particular stress methodology used to preserve those rights, which was
     developed and historically applied in a serial queue framework, can be carried into a
     simultaneous cluster without modification and still provide a reasonable measure of the
     transmission capability incrementally required by the new cluster.

9.   The difference between the serial and cluster settings is significant. In the serial process,
     the next project was studied against a base case reflecting applicable higher-queued
     projects and associated upgrades, so the effect of each successive queue position was
     isolated more directly. In the TCS, 23 equally queued projects were studied
     simultaneously and share responsibility for resulting upgrades. The CCIS analysis
     therefore can place the aggregate output of multiple TCS projects against the same
     deliberately stressed reference condition. A method that was reasonable in a serial
     process can produce a materially different result when the combined effect of 23 projects
     is added at once to a constraint that has been stressed to or near its limit. The difference
                                              PUBLIC VERSION
                                                                                             Attachment B
                                                                            Moraga Storage, et al. v. ISO-NE
                                                                                       Concentric Affidavit
                                                                                                Page 4 of 53

        makes the stress case construction and the incremental need identification especially
        important.

10.     The manner in which ISO-NE constructs the CCIS reference condition is therefore
        central to the causation inquiry. For each monitored constraint, ISO-NE identifies
        qualifying harmer resources and increases the applicable transfer until the monitored
        element reaches its applicable limit or the qualifying resources reach their established
        capacity capability. The TCS increment is then measured against that constructed
        reference condition. A positive DFAX and a post-cluster overload demonstrate that the
        TCS projects contribute to the studied condition.1 They do not, standing alone, establish
        that the projects caused the entire underlying transmission need or that the full scope of
        the resulting physical upgrade is incremental to the requested service.

11.     The magnitude of the TCS results makes this distinction consequential. The Final TCS
        Report identified approximately $3.17 billion in total interconnection costs for the 23
        projects, including approximately $2.51 billion in System Network Upgrades. Of those
        System Network Upgrade costs, approximately $2.16 billion is associated with thermal
        upgrades identified through the CCIS capacity-deliverability analysis. The principal cost
        issue addressed in this affidavit concerns approximately $2.16 billion of capacity-related
        thermal upgrades, representing approximately 86% of the System Network Upgrade costs
        identified in the Final TCS Report.2 Many of these capacity-related thermal upgrades are
        disputed.

12.     The disputed costs are concentrated at constraints with little or no remaining headroom
        before the TCS increment is introduced. Of 49 identified capacity-related violations, 33
        arise where reference DC loading exceeds 90%, and 14 arise where reference loading
        exceeds 99%. Using the final upgrade estimates, constraints above 90% account for
        approximately $1.83 billion, or 84.6%, of mapped CCIS-driven thermal upgrade costs,
        while the 14 constraints above 99% account for approximately $1.13 billion, or 52.6%.
        These results do not – by themselves – establish that upgrades are unnecessary, but
        indicate additional analysis is required before the upgrades are attributed solely to the
        TCS projects.

13.     The performance of the cluster reference condition is particularly important. ISO-NE’s
        reference loading analysis relies in part on DC screening, while AC power flow can
        produce materially different loading results because it reflects reactive power, voltage,
        and losses. The record indicates that at least one constraint was already overloaded in AC

        deficiency already exists before the TCS increment is introduced, the TCS projects may
        still require some incremental capability, but the existence of the pre-cluster deficiency

        solution is assigned to the cluster. Dispatch changes outside the stated DFAX threshold

14.     The geographic scope of the CCIS analysis raises a separate concern. The ISO-NE Open
        Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) defines the CCIS as an intra-zonal deliverability
        standard, and Planning Procedure 5-6 (“PP5-6”) identifies the relevant zones as Load
        Zones. An analysis prepared for the interconnection customers, which we have reviewed
        and find credible, identifies 23 TCS upgrades associated with Load Zone boundaries.4
        Thirteen, totaling approximately $378.8 million, are upgrades to facilities that cross a
        Load Zone boundary; the remaining ten, totaling approximately $572.0 million, were
        triggered in dispatch cases that stressed, or were bound by, a boundary facility. Together

        $717.5 million arises only in CCIS testing. That result warrants examination of whether

        capability beyond the intra-zonal deliverability obligation imposed by the CCIS.5

15.     The TCS results should also be capable of independent technical review and
        reproduction. Interconnection customers reported material reconciliation issues when
        attempting to reconstruct key study results using the seed cases, ISO-NE’s Dispatch

        used PowerGEM TARA Version 2503.3 for the CCIS analyses performed in the TCS.6

16.     Cost allocation and incremental causation are distinct issues. ISO-NE Tariff Schedule 11
        and PP5-6 specify how project-specific impacts are used to allocate the cost of an
        identified upgrade. Those allocation quantities do not represent a decomposition of a
        single physical study condition. ISO-NE’s own 381-ES example illustrates the
        distinction. [BEGIN CEII]

        proportional allocation cannot substitute for the determination of whether, and to what
        extent, the upgrade is incrementally required by the TCS projects.

17.     Our experience in other regions confirms methodological choices create these outcomes.
        The outcomes are not unavoidable consequences of protecting existing capacity rights
        during cluster studies. For instance, the New York Independent System Operator, Inc.
        (“NYISO”) recently revised its deliverability methodology after its first cluster analysis
        demonstrated that assumptions used to construct its deliverability analysis materially
        affected the transmission upgrades identified as necessary, and the Federal Energy
        Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) accepted those revisions. NYISO’s
        experience demonstrates that opportunities for testing and iteration can materially
        improve the methodology to determine the incremental requirements from
        interconnection customers.

18.   In sum, several interrelated features of the TCS methodology and process, in
      combination, create actual and plausible issues of whether most upgrades identified by
      ISO-NE have been properly identified as incremental requirements of the TCS projects:

      (a)    Application of the capacity deliverability methodology in a simultaneous cluster.
             ISO-NE applied a capacity deliverability methodology developed and historically
             used in a serial queue framework to 23 equally queued projects studied
             simultaneously with shared upgrade responsibility. Under that methodology, ISO-
             NE constructs constraint-specific stressed reference conditions before adding the
             TCS increment. In a cluster, the aggregate effects of multiple projects can cause a
             constraint with little or no remaining headroom to cross its study limit. The fact
             that the cluster causes that threshold crossing does not, itself, establish that the
             full scope of the resulting transmission solution is incrementally required by the
             cluster.

      (b)    Lack of AC verification of material pre-cluster conditions. ISO-NE relied in part
             on DC screening to identify capacity-related thermal constraints and performed
             AC verification only after an element was identified as overloaded. As a result,
             constraints at or near their applicable limits in the pre-cluster reference condition
             do not appear to have been tested in AC before the TCS increment was
             introduced. For those constraints, the applicable violation likely already exists in
             the modeled pre-cluster condition. The affected cases should therefore be tested in
             AC before the incremental TCS impact and resulting upgrade responsibility are
             determined.

      (c)    Inclusion of inter-zonal constraints in the CCIS analysis. The Tariff defines the
             CCIS deliverability obligation in terms of deliverability within the applicable
             Load Zone. Our analysis identifies material TCS upgrades for which the
             overloaded facility, stressed element, or binding constraint is located on a Load
             Zone boundary. If those inter-zonal constraints were used to establish
             transmission upgrades for which the TCS projects were assigned CCIS-related
             costs, the affected study cases must be reanalyzed using conditions consistent
             with the applicable intra-zonal deliverability requirement. This is not simply a
             matter of changing the allocation of an otherwise unchanged upgrade because the
             inter-zonal constraint may have affected the dispatch, binding condition, or
             upgrade identified in the first instance.

      (d)    Attribution of the full upgrade scope where the reference condition was already
             highly stressed. A substantial portion of the CCIS-driven upgrade cost arises from
             constraints that were already at or near their applicable limits before the TCS
             increment was introduced. Of the 49 identified capacity-related violations, 33 had
             reference loading above 90% and 14 had reference loading above 99%. Those 14
             constraints alone account for approximately $1.13 billion of mapped CCIS-driven
             thermal upgrade cost. Where a relatively small TCS increment causes an already
             highly stressed reference condition to cross a study limit, ISO-NE must separately
                                      PUBLIC VERSION

                                                                Moraga Storage, et al. v. ISO-NE
                                                                           Concentric Affidavit
                                                                                    Page 8 of 53

             determine whether the full physical upgrade is incrementally required by the TCS
             projects rather than treating the existence of the post-cluster violation as sufficient
             to establish responsibility for the full upgrade scope.

      (e)    Incomplete ability to reproduce material study results. Interconnection customers
             encountered material reconciliation issues when attempting to reconstruct TCS
             results using the materials ISO-NE provided. ISO-NE has not made its custom
             automation available to customers in a form that permits them to reproduce the
             material results. Until the relevant intermediate cases, conditioning steps, solver
             settings, implementation details, or applicable tools are provided, important
             questions concerning the construction of the reference cases and resulting
             constraints remain unresolved.

      (f)    Lack of a defined opportunity to retest material shared upgrades before
             commercial commitments become fixed. Although ISO-NE may conduct a restudy
             following project withdrawals, the determination whether to do so may occur only
             after remaining projects have entered interconnection agreements and posted
             substantial security. Where withdrawals materially change the projects
             contributing to a shared constraint, the affected upgrades should be retested before
             the remaining customers’ obligations become fixed.

19.   The principle underlying our opinions is straightforward. TCS customers should bear the
      cost of transmission facilities that are incrementally required to provide the
      interconnection service they request. They should not be assigned the full cost of a
      transmission solution merely because their projects are the final modeled increment that
      causes an already highly stressed constructed reference condition to cross a study limit.
      The same concern is even more pronounced where the AC reference case indicates that
      the relevant overload exists before the TCS projects are introduced. Before those costs
      become final, the record should demonstrate that the scope of the upgrade, and not simply
      the existence of the post-cluster violation, is incrementally attributable to the TCS
      projects. That inquiry can be performed while preserving reliability, protecting existing
      capacity rights, and allowing ISO-NE’s transition to the permanent cluster process to
      proceed.

II.   The Transition to Cluster Study and the TCS Results

      A.     Order No. 2023 and the Shift from Serial to Cluster Study

20.   Before ISO-NE implemented its FERC Order No. 2023 compliance provisions,
      interconnection requests were processed under a serial, “first-come, first-served”
      framework set out principally in Schedules 22 and 23 of the ISO-NE Tariff. Each
      interconnection request received a queue position based on the date it was submitted, and
      queue priority determined the sequence in which projects were studied in each study base
      case. A project was studied against the existing transmission system, applicable higher-
      queued projects, and the upgrades required by those higher-queued projects. ISO-NE then
                                             PUBLIC VERSION
                                                                                            Attachment B
                                                                           Moraga Storage, et al. v. ISO-NE
                                                                                      Concentric Affidavit
                                                                                               Page 9 of 53

        evaluated the incremental effect of the project under study and identified the additional
        transmission upgrades necessary to provide its requested interconnection service.

21.     Within that serial framework, the ISO evaluated two distinct levels of interconnection
        service. The first level, studied under the NCIS, evaluated the transmission upgrades
        necessary for Network Resource Interconnection Service (“NRIS”); NRIS allows a
        generating facility to participate as a Network Resource, but does not permit use as a
        capacity resource. The second level, studied under the CCIS and provided as CNRIS,
        addresses capacity deliverability and the upgrades necessary to establish Capacity
        Network Resource Capability (“CNRC”). Under the pre-Order No. 2023 framework,
        ISO-NE integrated the interconnection and Forward Capacity Market (“FCM”) processes.
        New resources could establish CNRC through the FCM qualification process and a
        Capacity Supply Obligation, subject to completion of required upgrades and other
        qualification requirements. Order No. 2023 reforms separate the establishment of
        CNRIS/CNRC from the FCM process.9

22.     The study assumptions and methodology for this capacity deliverability analysis are set
        out in PP5-6. By design, the PP5-6 deliverability construct is conservative. In general
        terms, it models a range of load and resource conditions, including a 90/10 forecast peak-
        load condition, and evaluates thermal, voltage, and stability performance under the
        contingencies specified by the procedure. For the TCS specifically, ISO-NE used the
        2025 CELT forecast and base cases that included in-service, under-construction, and
        planned transmission and generation projects expected to be in service by 2030. Under
        Section 3.1.1 of PP5-6, the maximum allowable post-contingency loading for N-1 and
        N-1-1 thermal analysis is the applicable Long Time Emergency (“LTE”) rating, and
        Section 3.2 of PP5-6 directs that steady-state analyses stress flows across the applicable
        lines and interfaces, to the extent reasonable, at or near the applicable rating or transfer
        limit. For CCIS, PP5-6 also specifies a reference-loading/redispatch construct intended to
        preserve established capacity deliverability before the incremental effect of the proposed
        generating facility or ETU is added. Accordingly, it is more precise to describe the
        analysis as a stressed capacity-deliverability test under prescribed scenarios than as a test
        requiring every capacity resource in an area to be delivered simultaneously at system
        peak.10

23.     Not every upgrade identified in the serial process was necessarily caused by, or assigned
        wholly to, a single project. The pre-Order No. 2023 Tariff included overlapping-impact
        and cost-allocation rules, and the actual responsibility for a particular upgrade depended
        on the applicable study and Tariff provisions.11 However, in the serial environment, the

        variables associated with each studied together with the compounding impacts of
        conservative assumptions.

24.     In Order No. 2023, FERC concluded that serial first-come, first-served interconnection
        processes had contributed to large queue backlogs and long study delays, in part because
        the existing framework did not sufficiently discourage speculative or non-viable requests
        and because withdrawals could require restudies and contribute to delay and cost
        uncertainty. The Commission therefore required transmission providers, including ISO-
        NE, to replace serial processing with a “first-ready, first-served” cluster study process.
        The relevant elements of that process are:12

        (a)     Simultaneous study. Valid interconnection requests submitted during a defined
                cluster request window are studied together in a single cluster study rather than
                one at a time in queue order.

        (b)     Shared network upgrade responsibility. System Network Upgrade costs identified
                in the cluster study are allocated among projects in the cluster as specified in ISO-
                NE’s Tariff.

        (c)     Readiness requirements. To enter and remain in the cluster process, an
                interconnection customer must satisfy site-control and financial/readiness
                requirements, including study and commercial-readiness deposits that become
                more substantial as the project advances.

        (d)     Withdrawal discipline. Order No. 2023 requires withdrawal penalties in specified
                circumstances when a withdrawal materially affects other requests in the cluster,
                with the penalty framework intended to deter non-viable projects and mitigate
                harm to remaining customers.

        (e)     Study deadlines. Order No. 2023 replaced the former reasonable-efforts standard
                with specified study deadlines backed by study-delay penalties, subject to the
                terms and exceptions adopted by the Commission.

       C.       Why the Transition Matters

29.    The PP5-6 capacity-deliverability construct was developed and historically applied
       within a serial queue framework in which projects retained queue priority, including in
       capacity group studies that evaluated requests in serial queue order. Applying that
       construct to 23 equally queued projects studied simultaneously and assigned shared
       responsibility for resulting upgrades changes how the methodology interacts with cost
       allocation and withdrawal. The process may not be appropriate in a cluster environment.
       The differences between serial and cluster analysis warrant careful examination for
       several reasons.

       (a)      Coincidence of assumed output. The relevant CCIS scenarios place the TCS
                projects into constraint-specific stressed conditions while preserving the
                deliverability associated with existing and higher-priority capacity resources. In
                the serial framework, the incremental transfer being tested ordinarily reflected the
                next project in queue. In the TCS, multiple equally queued projects within the
                applicable study area can be reflected simultaneously in the incremental transfer.
                The result is not simply the same test repeated for more projects. The aggregate
                incremental transfer applied against a deliberately stressed reference condition
                can be materially larger than the transfer associated with a single serial-queue
                project. That difference makes the construction of the reference condition, the
                treatment of the balancing generation, and the identification of incremental
                transmission needs materially more consequential.

       (b)      Shared cost responsibility. In the serial framework, projects were evaluated in
                queue order against a base case that incorporated applicable higher-queued
                projects and upgrades, so the incremental effect of each successive queue position
                was isolated more directly, although cost responsibility still depended on the
                applicable Tariff rules. In the cluster, multiple equally queued projects are studied
                together and shared upgrade costs are allocated by proportional impact. Each
                project’s cost depends on both its own impact and the composition of the cluster.

30.    These effects arise from applying the PP5-6 methodology in a materially different study
       and cost-allocation context. As applied in the TCS, incremental interconnection-driven
       needs are likely not distinguished from limitations embedded in the reference condition.
       The PP5-6 study methodology may no longer be reasonable in the context of cluster
       studies.

III.   The TCS Capacity Deliverability Methodology Does Not Reliably Isolate
       Incremental Cost Causation

       A.     The Question an Interconnection Study Must Answer

37.    An interconnection study serves an important purpose: to determine what changes to the
       transmission system are required to accommodate a proposed interconnection consistent
       with the applicable interconnection service and reliability standards. In a cluster study,
       that inquiry requires answering three related but separate questions, in sequence:
       (i) whether a transmission limitation or need exists under the pre-existing conditions;
       (ii) to what extent that need is incrementally caused by the interconnection requests under
       study; and (iii) if an upgrade is incrementally required by those requests, how its cost
       should be allocated among the projects and load that contribute to the need. Each
       question depends on the one before it. Cost allocation cannot correct an error in
       identifying the need, and a need that exists without the cluster does not become an
       incremental need simply because cluster projects contribute to it.

38.    ISO-NE did not properly complete the first two steps in the TCS, and the third step
       inherited the resulting errors. Primarily, ISO-NE carried a capacity-deliverability
       methodology developed and historically applied within a serial queue framework into its
       first full cluster study, without adapting it to a setting in which 23 projects are studied
       simultaneously against the same reference condition. At the first step, ISO-NE identified
       capacity-related needs under reference conditions constructed by increasing transfers
       until monitored elements reached their limits. ISO-NE only screened reference conditions
       in DC, and AC verification was performed only after the TCS projects were added, so
       ISO-NE did not determine whether constraints at or near their limits already violated
       criteria before the cluster was introduced. In addition, 23 of the upgrades identified were
       associated with Load Zone boundaries, beyond the intra-zonal deliverability the CCIS is
       intended to test. The limitations identified are beyond the limitations the CCIS requires
       the TCS projects to address. At the second step, ISO-NE treated the existence of a post-

      transmission system before the TCS projects are added, subject to the topology, load,
      generation, higher-priority projects, planned facilities, and other assumptions
      incorporated into that model. ISO-NE then performs the case conditioning and other
      study-specific adjustments to develop the cases used for the TCS analysis. The seed case
      is ISO-NE’s starting point; it should not be equated with the reference condition
      ultimately used to measure the incremental capacity impact of the TCS projects.

53.   Second, ISO-NE evaluates monitored transmission elements under the applicable system
      conditions and contingencies. For example, ISO-NE may evaluate loading on
      Transmission Line A following the loss of Transmission Line B. Because power flows
      redistribute when a transmission facility is removed from service, the effect of a
      particular generator on Line A may be different following the loss of Line B than it is

      element. ISO-NE does this using distribution factors, or DFAX, which measure the

      particular resource. A positive DFAX indicates that increasing the output of the resource
      increases flow on the monitored element under the applicable system condition and
      contingency. A negative DFAX indicates that increasing the resource’s output reduces
      flow on the monitored element.

        E.      Why the TCS Methodology Raises But For Causation and Cost
                Responsibility Questions

64.     The significance of the reference case is ultimately a question of causation and cost
        responsibility. Schedule 11 does not provide that TCS projects are responsible for the
        cost of an upgrade merely because their addition produces or contributes to a modeled
        overload. Rather, Schedule 11 ties interconnection cost responsibility to costs that would
        not have been incurred but for the interconnection.31 The relevant inquiry is whether, and
        to what extent, the cost of the identified transmission upgrade would have been incurred
        absent the TCS projects.

65.     ISO-NE begins with the pre-TCS seed case and then applies study-specific case
        conditioning, modeling assumptions, and the reference transfer to establish the condition
        against which the TCS projects are evaluated. That process can leave a monitored
        element at or near its applicable limit before the TCS projects are added. The subsequent
        addition of the TCS projects may demonstrate that those projects contribute incremental
        loading beyond that reference condition, but it does not necessarily establish that the full
        scope of the resulting transmission upgrade is incrementally required by those projects.
        The relevant question is whether the identified upgrade, and the transmission capability it
        provides, is required because of the TCS increment rather than because of conditions
        already reflected in the constructed reference case.

66.     The distinction between transmission conditions that exist before the TCS increment is
        introduced and transmission needs that arise because of the TCS projects is critical. Each
        identified upgrade that was required without the TCS interconnections should be assigned
        to load.

101.    NYISO’s experience demonstrates empirically that assumptions used to construct a
        capacity-deliverability counterfactual can materially affect whether an interconnection
        study identifies major transmission upgrades as necessary. A power-flow model may
        accurately calculate the electrical consequences of the system condition it is instructed to
        analyze. But whether that result demonstrates an incremental transmission need
        attributable to the new resources depends on whether the condition being modeled
        reasonably represents the transmission capability necessary to provide the requested
        interconnection service.

102.    The distinction is relevant to the incremental-causation issue discussed above. ISO-NE’s
        PP5-6 methodology constructs a reference condition intended to preserve the capacity
        network capability associated with existing and higher-priority resources before
        measuring the incremental effect of the TCS resources. A positive DFAX and an increase
        in loading after the TCS resources are introduced demonstrate that those resources
        contribute to the modeled constraint. The additional question is whether the reference
        condition appropriately distinguishes the transmission capability that must be preserved
        for pre-existing resources and system conditions from the additional transmission
        capability required because the TCS projects receive CNRIS.

103.    PP5-6, as applied in the TCS, does not adequately distinguish between transmission
        capability required to preserve existing capacity rights and transmission capability
        incrementally required to provide CNRIS to the TCS projects. Unlike NYISO’s revised
        methodology, PP5-6 does not limit the assumed transfer by reference to the load that
        must actually be served on the receiving side of the constraint. Where application of that
        sink results in a transfer across a Load Zone boundary, PP5-6 also does not limit the
        modeled transfer by reference to the transmission capability necessary to make the TCS
        resources deliverable within their own Load Zone. As a result, the methodology can
        create a modeled transfer across a constrained element that exceeds the transfer necessary
        to provide the requested CNRIS. An overload produced by that assumed transfer
        establishes that the system cannot accommodate the modeled transfer; it does not,
        without further analysis, establish that the same transmission capability or resulting
        Network Upgrade is incrementally required by the TCS projects. Thus, the TCS
        methodology does not reliably distinguish the transmission need associated with the
        modeled transfer from the transmission capability incrementally required to provide the

       A.     Simultaneous Study and Shared Upgrades

117.   Five features of the capacity-deliverability analysis bear on the TCS results. None is
       necessarily problematic standing alone. Their significance in the TCS arises from the fact
       that multiple equally queued projects are evaluated simultaneously against the same
       constraint-specific reference conditions and share responsibility for resulting upgrades.
       That structure makes the construction of the reference condition, the amount of remaining
       headroom, the treatment of project impacts, and the ability to revisit the results after the
       cluster changes more consequential than they were in the serial process.

       (a)    Constraint-specific stressing. The deliverability analysis does not test the system
              under a single dispatch. For each monitored constraint, it constructs a dispatch
              that stresses that constraint, generally by increasing output from resources that
              load it and reducing output from resources that relieve it. Each constraint is thus
              tested under the dispatch that is most adverse to it, even though those dispatches
              differ from one another and would not all occur at once.

       (b)    Preservation of existing capacity rights. Resources that already hold capacity
              network resource capability are modeled so that their deliverability is preserved.
              A new resource is not permitted to rely on transfer capability that the analysis
              treats as needed to deliver existing capacity, whether or not that existing capacity
              is likely to operate at full output under the stressed condition, and whether or not
              it is likely to remain in service.

       (c)    Limited headroom. Because of the first two features, the transfer capability
              available to new resources on a given constraint is only the margin that remains
              after existing capacity has been dispatched to stress that constraint. As discussed
              in Section IV, on some constraints that margin is small or nonexistent before any
              new project is added. That is not an occasional condition in the TCS. Of the 49
              identified violations, 33 arise at constraints whose reference loading already
              exceeded 90%, and 14 at constraints already above 99%; those 14 constraints
              alone carry $1.13 billion of capacity-related upgrade cost. In addition, as
              previously discussed, this limited headroom creates a condition where the
              difference between DC screening analysis and AC power flow can mask the
              situation where a transmission element is already in violation in the reference
              case, before the TCS resources are considered.

       (d)    Simultaneous cluster injections. In a cluster, the TCS projects are modeled
              together. A project’s effect on a particular stressed constraint depends on its
              DFAX under the applicable study condition; only projects meeting the applicable
              association and cost-allocation criteria are assigned responsibility for that
              violation or upgrade.

132.     Under the Tariff, Network Upgrades identified for an interconnection request are funded

VIII. Recommended Methodological and Targeted Transitional Relief

137.   Any remedy should preserve reliability and existing capacity rights while ensuring that
       TCS customers are assigned only those transmission facilities incrementally required to
       provide their requested interconnection service. In our opinion, that requires correction of
       the methodological issues identified above before the disputed capacity-related upgrade
       allocations are finalized. In particular, the TCS analysis should: (i) respect established
       transfer capabilities across Load Zone boundaries; (ii) distinguish violations that exist in
       the reference condition from those caused by the TCS projects; (iii) account appropriately
       for transmission facilities that are already subject to planned asset condition work; and
       (iv) use generation dispatch assumptions that represent reasonably stressed conditions
       consistent with the applicable ISO-NE Planning Procedures. The objective is not to
       substitute economic dispatch for conservative reliability analysis. It is to ensure that the
       conditions used to protect existing reliability and capacity rights are not themselves
       treated as incremental transmission needs caused by the TCS projects.

138.     First, the CCIS analysis should respect established transfer capabilities across existing
         Load Zone boundaries. PP5-6 provides that a generating facility seeking CCIS is not
         responsible for increasing the transfer capability of interfaces forming the boundaries

         worst imaginable extreme. PP5-3 defines reasonably stressed conditions as severe load

         6 expressly incorporates that definition.68

IX.    Conclusion

145.   The central issue presented by the TCS is whether the transmission upgrades assigned to
       the TCS projects have been shown to be incrementally required to provide the
       interconnection service those projects request. ISO-NE appropriately uses stressed
       conditions to preserve existing capacity rights, and the simultaneous study of multiple
       equally queued projects is an expected feature of cluster study. The concern is that the
       TCS record does not reliably distinguish transmission need already reflected in the
       constructed reference conditions from the additional transmission capability
       incrementally required by the TCS projects.

146.   Of approximately $3.17 billion in total interconnection costs identified in the Final TCS
       Report, approximately $2.16 billion is associated with thermal upgrades identified
       through the capacity-deliverability analysis rather than the energy-level analysis. The
       disputed costs are concentrated at constraints with very little remaining headroom before
       the TCS increment is introduced. Of the 49 identified capacity-related violations, 33 arise
       at constraints with reference loading above 90% and 14 arise above 99%. Constraints
       above 90% account for approximately $1.83 billion, or 84.6%, of the approximately
       $2.16 billion in mapped CCIS-driven thermal-upgrade costs, while the 14 constraints
       above 99% account for approximately $1.13 billion, or 52.6%. These results do not
       establish that those upgrades are unnecessary. They do demonstrate why the existence of
       a post-TCS violation, standing alone, is insufficient to establish that the full scope of the
       resulting upgrade is an incremental requirement of the TCS projects.

147.   ISO-NE’s methodology also uses different analytical constructs to establish the CCIS
       reference condition and to measure project-specific impacts for cost allocation. The
       resulting allocation quantities are not necessarily an additive decomposition of the
       incremental physical flow produced by the cluster. Determining which projects share the
       cost of an identified upgrade is therefore a different question from determining whether,
       and to what extent, the upgrade itself is required because of those projects.

148.   Several unresolved factual questions bear directly on that determination. For highly
       stressed constraints, the record does not consistently establish whether the applicable
       violation exists in AC before the TCS increment is introduced because the reference-
       condition screening was performed in DC and AC verification was performed only after
       an overload was identified. Questions also remain concerning the construction of
       particular reference cases, including dispatch changes outside the stated DFAX threshold
       and the treatment of resources that relieve or increase loading on the monitored
       constraint. Interconnection customers have also reported material difficulties reproducing
       certain TCS results using the cases and replication materials ISO-NE provided. In
       addition, project withdrawals can change both the projects contributing to a shared
       constraint and the transmission capability required by the remaining cluster. Each of

CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER


Ms. Powers has over 35 years of experience in the energy industry with specific expertise in the

the design, implementation, and operation of installed capacity markets across North America.
She has experience in electric resource planning, including assessing the costs and benefits of
